title: How Trump’s FBI Purge Saved Lindsey Graham and James Clyburn From a Bribery Investigation
author: Kirsten Berg
content:
On March 3, 2020, Sen. Lindsey Graham walked into a private dining room at
Charlie Palmer Steak in Washington, D.C. Graham’s time was expensive. He was
meeting with two executives and a lobbyist from a Hawaiian naval defense
contractor called Navatek. And he had required them to commit to $40,000 in
campaign contributions for a 45-minute meeting.

Navatek’s CEO, Martin Kao, was confident that was all the time he needed.

“Shoot all he has to really do is stop by and say ‘yes,’” Kao wrote to a
Navatek lobbyist and a fellow executive the day before, in an email seen by
ProPublica. “That should only take a minute and he’s on his way. We don’t need
to pretend we give a shit about each other.”

At the dinner, Graham ate little and talked a lot. But Kao got the “yes” he
was hoping for: Graham agreed to steer a $10 million government contract
Navatek’s way in his native South Carolina, Kao later recounted to the FBI. In
exchange, he said, Graham asked Kao to pledge a total of $100,000 to his
reelection campaign.

### “Paper Trail” Podcast

Hear the reporters discuss their reporting on the FBI on ”Paper Trail.”

In early 2025, the FBI opened a sweeping investigation into bribery on Capitol
Hill with Graham’s steakhouse dinner at the center. Kao confessed to federal
agents that his business model consisted of bribing public officials in
exchange for government contracts, and that the research Navatek was providing
to the government was often worthless.

The scheme involved some of the most powerful figures in Congress, he said —
in both parties. In South Carolina, Kao told agents, Navatek made a campaign
cash-for-contracts deal not only with Graham, but also with the state’s top
Democrat, Rep. James Clyburn, and another influential Republican, Rep. Joe
Wilson.

Kao told agents that Graham in particular left little room for ambiguity:
“This is how much I want, and how much I am going to give you,” Kao remembered
Graham saying, according to notes one agent took during their debrief in late
2024.

Kao’s admissions would constitute a vast criminal bribery scheme if they could
be proved in court — a challenge, given recent [Supreme Court
rulings](https://fixthecourt.com/2024/07/recent-supreme-court-cases-that-
license-corruption/) that have made it more difficult to win corruption cases.
Kao himself posed another hurdle. He was facing prison for fraud and campaign
finance violations and was speaking to the FBI in the hopes of reducing his
sentence.

But the FBI agents who took Kao’s confession — two experienced anti-corruption
investigators — could see that much of it lined up with a trove of records
they had seized from Navatek. They forged ahead. The FBI took the formal step
of naming two former Navatek executives who had worked with Kao as subjects of
a bribery investigation. The agency did not designate Graham, Clyburn and
Wilson that way, but the agents were actively investigating their interactions
with Kao. The agents indicated to their superiors that the lawmakers could
become subjects in the future, according to records viewed by ProPublica.

The details of this investigation have not previously been reported.

President Donald Trump returned to the White House and almost immediately
gutted the specialized FBI and Department of Justice teams dedicated to taking
on public corruption — an act of revenge for having previously investigated
him. The two experienced agents on the case were swept up in the purge, and
the career prosecutor assisting them quit after Trump appointees forbid the
DOJ’s anti-corruption section from filing [any new
cases](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/how-trump-defanged-justice-
departments-political-corruption-watchdogs-2025-06-09/). Today, there is no
one left to look into Kao’s explosive allegations, as the Trump administration
has abandoned any pretense of prosecuting public corruption. The case is dead.

ProPublica has unearthed the investigation by reviewing thousands of pages of
legal documents, internal company emails, evidence the FBI used to vet Kao’s
claims and dozens of interviews with people who saw how Navatek operated,
including an eyewitness to Graham and Kao’s secret steakhouse dinner.

This story is part of a series based on our reporting. Last month, [ProPublica
reported](https://www.propublica.org/article/fbi-susan-collins-navatek-
campaign-donations-investigation) that the FBI had probed the conduct of Maine
Sen. Susan Collins, who steered millions in government funding toward Navatek
while Kao gave her illegal campaign donations. Collins denied wrongdoing and
dismissed Kao as a “convicted liar.”

Kao is indeed the only person involved to serve prison time. He pleaded guilty
to making illegal campaign donations and a loan fraud scheme in 2022. In 2025,
he was sentenced to 87 months in prison.

Graham died at 71 earlier this year. His sister, Darline Graham, who was
appointed to fill his seat, retained most of his senior staff, including those
who dealt with Navatek. She even took up some of his committee assignments,
including appropriations. Darline Graham is running for a full term in office
this November.

Clyburn, 86, is one of the most powerful Democrats in Washington. He is widely
credited with tipping the scales for Joe Biden during the 2020 Democratic
presidential primary. Wilson remains influential on national defense spending
from his senior perch on the Armed Services Committee.

![Two political figures visit during an event at the White House. The
individual on the left gestures while speaking, while the other individual
listens and smiles. On the far right of the image, there is an out-of-focus
soldier in a formal uniform.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2170516370.jpg?w=752)James Clyburn, left,
and Lindsey Graham speak during an event at the White House to celebrate the
2023-24 University of South Carolina Gamecocks NCAA women’s basketball
championship team. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

“Whatever a donor may think or say, a donation would never cause Congressman
Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Jami LaRue,
Clyburn’s communications director, wrote in response to detailed questions.
“The Congressman has always striven to assist the University of South Carolina
and all of the colleges and universities in his district when called upon to
further their important missions. The crimes and lies of an imprisoned
fraudster will not cause the Congressman to waver in his support for these
fine institutions.”

David Snider, Wilson’s communications director, did not address a detailed
list of questions sent by ProPublica. “Congressman Wilson does and has always
abided by campaign donation regulations set forth by the Federal Election
Commission,” Snider said in an email.

In an emailed statement, Taylor Reidy, who was Lindsey Graham’s communications
director and now holds the same post for his sister, wrote that “any
allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior or wrongdoing by the late Senator Lindsey
Graham or his staff are simply false.” She said the accusations were the
“ravings of a convicted felon” and that her office was never contacted by the
FBI about the matter. After Kao’s arrest, they disgorged his donations, she
added.

The two executives who were subjects of the FBI investigation, Duke Hartman
and Joshua Knight, were never charged. Hartman, the other executive at the
dinner meeting with Graham, is now the CEO of a new naval research company
called Integer Technologies that he co-founded with Knight after Kao’s arrest.
Integer was recently recognized as one of the [fastest-growing government
contractors](https://www.integer-tech.com/integer-technologies-ranks-no-95-on-
the-2025-inc-5000-list-of-americas-fastest-growing-private-companies/) in the
country. It also became the ultimate beneficiary of the Graham dinner meeting,
picking up the contract Graham allegedly agreed to facilitate that night.

Hartman and Knight did not respond to detailed requests for comment.

“[It’s] corruption at its best,” Kao wrote to ProPublica from federal
detention in South Dakota, before cutting off contact. “But I am the only one
rotting in prison.”

### Small Company, Big Ambitions

Kao’s dinner with Graham was part of his grandiose plan to make Navatek a
major defense contractor.

He had become the CEO at an uncertain moment in the company’s history. Founded
in Hawaii in the 1970s, the company originally thrived on a close relationship
with the state’s powerful senior senator, Daniel Inouye. When Kao assumed
ownership in 2019, it had been several years since Inouye had died, and
Navatek was in need of a new patron in Washington.

At times, Kao hardly seemed the person to pull this off. He had started out as
the company’s CFO and was openly uninterested in its technology. He told
bombastic lies about his personal life. Former employees said he regaled them
with tales of selling newspapers for members of the Bloods and Crips street
gangs as a youth. In a deposition, Kao later admitted that wasn’t true.

But what he lacked in engineering chops he made up with ambition. Once, Kao
held a company town hall using a map of the U.S. dotted with future Navatek
offices as his backdrop, a former employee recalled. “He would talk about how
we’re a $10 million company, and in the next three years, we’re going to be a
billion-dollar company,” said a former engineer. “He was an absolute
megalomaniac.”

Kao hatched a plan to expand Navatek’s presence across the country, making new
friends in Congress along the way. He courted politicians using something he
called “the method,” as [ProPublica detailed in
September](https://www.propublica.org/article/fbi-susan-collins-navatek-
campaign-donations-investigation).

Navatek would open an office in the state or district of a powerful member of
Congress and partner with a local university to concoct a proposal for
federally funded research. Then, aided by a well-connected lobbyist and the
sheen of credibility from its association with the university, Navatek would
approach the member for federal research funding.

Kao told the FBI he would strike deals in small, face-to-face meetings with
the members or their trusted staff. Navatek — through executives, family
members and lobbyists — would make generous campaign donations. In exchange,
the member would add detailed language to the defense budget to fund the
company’s work.

That legislative language would not name the company. But it would describe
specific work that Navatek was already planning to do behind the scenes,
making it the only logical choice for the eventual government contract. The
lawmakers’ staff would also backchannel with the Navy after the bill was
passed to make sure contracting offices knew to direct the money to Navatek,
emails seen by ProPublica show — even though the contracts were in theory
competitive.

Kao “wanted to build a company as big as he could as fast as he could,” a
former executive later testified in court. For a while, he succeeded. Under
Kao, Navatek went from having to “rebuild,” as the executive put it, to
winning $40.7 million in new government contracts in 2020.

Hartman, the other Navatek executive who went to dinner with Graham, was in
charge of maintaining friendly ties in Congress while tracking the millions of
dollars the company had requested in research funds. He kept careful tabs on
the company’s progress using dozens of color-coded spreadsheets. “If anyone
knows the impropriety of the business model, it’s him,” Kao told the FBI,
referring to Hartman.

Later, these spreadsheets provided the FBI a detailed picture of which
congressional offices worked closest with Navatek. In the tables devoted to
South Carolina, Navatek denoted Graham as a “key supporter.”

The company primarily targeted lawmakers from smaller states who sat on
appropriations committees, like Collins, Kao explained to the FBI, because
they wielded huge power over the budget while having fewer “constituents to
‘feed.’”

The senior senator from South Carolina was another prime target. “You can get
access to Lindsey Graham,” Eric Schiff, a former Navatek executive, said in an
interview.

Kao, Hartman and other Navatek executives approached the offices of Graham,
Clyburn and Wilson — all powerful members of the South Carolina delegation —
in the beginning of 2019. The company had recruited the University of South
Carolina for a joint research project, and together they asked the lawmakers
to find $9.5 million to fund the work. If it succeeded, Navatek planned to ask
Congress to re-up the funding for two more years as well as green-light two
more projects, internal company records show, for a total of up to $90 million
in South Carolina alone.

Yet Navatek had “zero people” capable of doing the research it was pitching,
said a former executive with direct knowledge of the work.

Its $9.5 million “power and energy” proposal promised cutting-edge research on
how to distribute the limited power on board a ship between multiple energy-
intense systems, like radars, lasers and rail guns. Graham’s office later
boasted that the work would lead to new technology that would “ensure that our
fleet is ready for the fights of the future.”

In reality, Navatek’s initial research “looked like a college senior’s
graduation project,” the executive said. “Something you go get from
RadioShack.” Graham’s office referred questions about the quality of the work
to the Navy and the university. The Office of Naval Research, which awarded
the contract, did not respond to questions.

![A futuristic large tank-like vehicle comes out of the water onto a beach
under a cloudy sky and against a background of rocky cliffs. A single
individual rides on top of the vehicle.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/aaa.jpg?w=1149)A Navatek amphibious vehicle prototype
heads to shore during a Marine Corps experiment in Hawaii in 2014. Lance Cpl.
Aaron S. Patterson/U.S. Marine Corps

But for Congress, that lack of expertise wasn’t a problem. Throughout 2019,
the FBI noted, as the ensuing year’s budget came together, both Graham’s and
Clyburn’s offices took steps to make sure it included Navatek’s funding.

In May 2019, Willie Lyles III, Clyburn’s legislative director, alerted Navatek
that the House Appropriations Committee would endorse new funding for a
“modular and scalable integrated power and thermal system capable of powering
a directed energy weapon system of 100 or more kilowatts,” according to an
email flagged by the FBI. Three days later, that exact language appeared in
the [House Appropriations Committee
report](https://www.congress.gov/committee-report/116th-congress/house-
report/84). Lyles did not reply to a request for comment.

In September, the Senate Appropriations Committee — Graham’s committee —
released a budget
[report](https://www.congress.gov/116/crpt/srpt103/CRPT-116srpt103.pdf#page=198)
that set aside $9.5 million in funding for “Talent and Technology for Navy
Power and Energy Systems.” Agents noted that Navatek may have ghostwritten the
technical description that accompanied this line item because “an almost
identical paragraph” appeared in Hartman’s internal spreadsheets two months
before the Senate report became public.  
  
After the Senate advanced its version of the budget in the fall, Navatek
dropped $4,799 to send bourbon to a handful of lawmakers, including Graham and
Collins, the FBI found in company records — a likely violation of Senate gift
rules. Both Collins’ and Graham’s offices denied receiving bourbon. Navatek
later sent Clyburn a fruit basket from Edible Arrangements for $102.60.

Congress passed the final spending bill containing $9.5 million for Navatek’s
pet project on Dec. 19, 2019.

At that point, Kao and other Navatek executives had not made any donations to
Clyburn, Wilson or even Graham.

That would change within days of Congress passing the budget, when an
executive pledged $750 to Wilson’s campaign at a fundraiser held at
Bullfeathers, a Capitol Hill watering hole for lobbyists and Hill staffers,
emails show. In the following weeks, Kao and his lobbyist gave Wilson’s
campaign $3,500.

And bigger checks were imminent. Kao kicked off 2020 by making plans to spend
$300,000 at a slew of political fundraisers, according to text messages filed
in court and a recent deposition. Navatek’s lobbyists at that time were
seeking private meetings with Graham, Wilson and Clyburn, where Kao planned to
ask for significantly more federal funding. Kao eventually met with all three,
and each asked for $100,000, he told the FBI.

During that same period, Kao and Hartman met a top fundraiser for Collins at a
Corner Bakery in Washington, D.C. [As ProPublica
reported](https://www.propublica.org/article/debunking-susan-collins-fbi-
navatek-investigation-claims), that meeting led Kao to donate $150,000 to the
pro-Collins super PAC. Kao told the FBI that the money was a bribe in exchange
for the senator’s support for more Navatek funding. The head of the super PAC
and Collins have denied Kao’s version of events.

Kao told the FBI it was not unusual for donations to come after the favor: “We
became clever in our own right and figured out how to dangle the carrot,” he
wrote in a memo seen by ProPublica, “until we saw some assurance that the Ask
was in the budget.”

To secure a meeting with Graham, Kao hired Michael Tongour, a veteran South
Carolina lobbyist who was old law school friends with the senator and family
friends with Clyburn and Wilson. Graham was up for reelection against a well-
funded challenger, Jaime Harrison, and had a crowded fundraising schedule,
said Tongour, but they eventually found a time.

“The Graham fundraiser says that it [sic] you want to reserve a date for
Senator Graham to attend a private dinner, the campaign wants to get $40,000
in contributions,” Tongour wrote to Kao, Hartman and lobbyist Andy Winer, in
an undated email seen by ProPublica. Winer, whom Kao described as Navatek’s
chief lobbyist, chimed in to say that Graham could stay only 45 minutes, and
Kao replied that all they needed to hear was “yes.”

“These discussions are very frank and oddly not at all awkward,” Kao told the
FBI. “I suppose once we got that far, everyone knows the deal.”

### A Dinner With Graham

Graham showed up late to his March 3, 2020, dinner with Kao, Hartman and
Tongour. A fundraiser working for Graham appeared first and accepted an
envelope from Kao containing checks made out to Graham’s campaign, Kao said.
Kao did not know the fundraiser’s name; in an FBI debrief, he simply referred
to the person as the “money man.” After that person departed, Graham entered.

Graham, Kao recalled to the FBI, was “very abrupt” and “straight to the
point”: He asked how much Navatek wanted, to which they said $10 million a
year for three years. Graham asked Kao to pledge $100,000 in donations in
exchange for his support, Kao told the FBI.

Navatek was juggling multiple proposals in South Carolina worth around $10
million, and it’s not clear which one Kao was describing.

Congress had just approved the $9.5 million for the power and energy project,
but Navatek still needed the Navy to award the money in the form of a
contract. The company was also about to ask Congress to fund the same project
for a second year at $10.5 million. On top of that, Navatek was planning to
pitch a new research proposal, at $10 million, to study the transport of
supplies inland from ships using autonomous vehicles. It was another area
where Navatek had “zero past performance,” the former executive said.

The same week of the steakhouse dinner, Graham’s office was working behind the
scenes with Navatek and the University of South Carolina to make sure the Navy
sent the first $9.5 million to the right company.

A day before the dinner, an official with the Office of Naval Research emailed
Graham’s office to ask about the money, which “the Senator may have an
interest in.” Craig Abele, Graham’s national security adviser, called her a
few days later to confirm that Graham’s office had intended the money to be
awarded to the Navatek partnership, emails show. “Spoke to ONR this morning,”
Abele wrote March 6. “Should be set.”

The company received the contract, which it split with the university, in July
2020.

Abele became Graham’s deputy chief of staff and still holds the position for
Darline. He did not reply to an email requesting comment. A Graham
spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that their office had indeed added the
$9.5 million to the budget at the request of the university and Navatek. The
spokesperson said the research was supported by the Navy and rejected the
notion that Graham was motivated by campaign cash.

Graham’s spokesperson said requiring a fundraising minimum for a dinner was
normal practice.

> “[It’s] corruption at its best. But I am the only one rotting in prison.”
>
> Former Navatek CEO Martin Kao

The checks Kao handed over at the dinner added up to about half of the $40,000
he had agreed to raise for the dinner, according to Tongour. The rest came in
May, campaign records show.

“My understanding at the time was that the contributions associated with the
event were lawful political contributions,” Winer said. “I never advised Kao
to make a political contribution in exchange for official action. I never
participated in, witnessed or had knowledge of any illegal political
contribution.”

After Kao’s 2020 indictment, the University of South Carolina broke off the
partnership. **“** University officials were not aware of any political
contributions from Navatek,” Jeff Stensland, a university spokesperson, wrote
in an email. “Our sole objective in partnering with them was to expand our
research enterprise.”

One week after the dinner, on March 10, a University of South Carolina
lobbyist sent written requests to Graham’s office for $20.5 million in
appropriations: $10.5 million to continue Navatek’s power and energy research
and $10 million for its new autonomous vehicle research.

Tongour confirmed many elements of Kao’s story. In a recent interview with
ProPublica and subsequent emails, he remembered Kao giving the envelope full
of checks to Graham’s fundraiser and even agreed that Graham kept the meeting
short. “I don’t recall that he stayed more than 30 minutes,” Tongour said in
an email. “Certainly not for appetizers, entrée, and dessert.”

But he denied Kao’s most significant claim: that Graham and Navatek struck an
explicit, potentially illegal deal for contracts.

“I would remember that forever,” Tongour said. Graham supported Navatek’s
requests, he said, because they were good for the state. “If I had seen that
kind of quid pro quo, I would have quit earlier.” Tongour fired Navatek as a
client later that year, immediately after Kao’s arrest.

Navatek considered Graham its chief patron in South Carolina, internal records
show, just as it viewed Collins in Maine. But the company also wanted support
in the House.

For that, Navatek turned to Clyburn, a member of Democratic party leadership
and one of the most powerful figures in Congress. Agents found Navatek emails
setting a meeting with Clyburn for early March. The goal, Kao said, was to
make sure that the House draft of the budget “mirrored” whatever Graham
inserted in the Senate version.

Over a meal, Clyburn asked Kao how much he was donating to Graham and then
asked for the same amount, $100,000, Kao told the FBI.

The FBI tallied $20,000 in contributions that Kao and his family members made
to Clyburn a few days after their scheduled meeting. A month later, Hartman
arranged for a $10,000 gift to Clyburn’s alma mater, South Carolina State
University, according to an email seen by ProPublica. Hartman noted it was
“Congressman Clyburn’s favorite school.”

The spokesperson for Clyburn confirmed the dinner occurred but did not respond
to questions about what was discussed.

Kao and Hartman struck a similar bargain with Wilson, Kao told the FBI, at a
private lunch he secured by donating to his campaign. The FBI pulled records
of $3,500 in donations Kao and Tongour made in late 2019 and early 2020.

Wilson has an influential role on the House Armed Services Committee, which
authorizes defense spending. Wilson was “very clear and knew what the ask
was,” Kao told the FBI. He wanted however much Clyburn was getting in campaign
contributions in exchange for his support, Kao said.

Tongour denied this. “There was no ‘pay to play’ with Joe Wilson or his staff
either,” he wrote in an email, adding that he donated because Wilson “is a
friend and I want to see him re-elected.”

Kao claimed to the FBI that he paid for meals with all three politicians, but
campaign finance records appear to show the lawmakers’ campaigns picked up the
check.

By August 2020, Hartman had gotten word that Graham’s and Wilson’s committees
would each support part of the company’s requests, internal company records
show. Clyburn was not on key committees while he was a party leader. In one of
his myriad spreadsheets, Hartman projected that the final budget could include
up to $15.5 million of the $20.5 million the company had lobbied for.

Kao told agents he was gearing up to make more significant donations to
Graham, Clyburn and Wilson by the end of the year. Instead, on Sept. 30, 2020,
he was arrested.

Kao reflected on his time at Navatek in a deposition taken last month inside a
federal prison. The company’s founder has sued Kao, saying his stewardship
defrauded Navatek of millions.

“It’s nothing more than government contracting done through placating senior
appropriation members for contracts,” Kao said. “The whole thing is a grand
lie.”

### An Arrest, a Lifeboat

Kao’s arrest plunged Navatek into disarray. Federal prosecutors charged him
with defrauding a federal loan program; not long after, he was also charged
with making illegal donations to the Collins campaign and super PAC.
Lobbyists, universities and congressional offices abruptly cut off contact.
“Don’t call us,” one congressional office told an executive, he later
testified.

The Collins campaign said it disgorged Kao’s contribution. Yet the senator,
facing a tight reelection bid, has had to field questions following the
ProPublica report about her support for Navatek and why the super PAC
supporting her accepted the $150,000 donation from the shell company in the
first place.

As Navatek sank, Hartman began building himself a lifeboat. In 2021, he and
Knight started a new military research company headquartered in South Carolina
called Integer Technologies. Integer’s first project was one that Navatek had
brokered with Graham.

Hartman didn’t face any criminal charges at the time and left Navatek largely
unscathed. He would later settle a civil lawsuit brought by his former
employer, which contended he played a role in Kao’s campaign finance and loan
fraud schemes, for $425,000. He admitted no wrongdoing.

In September 2024, FBI agents flew to Hawaii for what would be their final
interview with Kao. They pressed him for details about what happened in South
Carolina, quizzing him on his dinner with Graham and a second in-person
meeting he said he had with Clyburn. Agents wanted Kao to help them find more
records that would back up his account and asked him to point them toward
lobbyists in D.C. who he said facilitated the pay-for-play scheme.

As the year came to a close, FBI agent Michelle Ball felt she had enough
material to move forward. The FBI had “uncovered a lengthy history” of a
government contractor making donations “in exchange for government contracts,”
she wrote in a Dec. 9, 2024, memo viewed by ProPublica.

In federal corruption probes, agents often begin by focusing on lower-level
targets with a goal of working their way up to more prominent figures. Ball
named Hartman; his business partner, Knight; and their company, Integer, as
the formal subjects of the probe, as they prepared to potentially issue
subpoenas and gather more evidence. They had Graham, Clyburn and Wilson in
their sights. Ball devoted entire sections of the memo to detailing the
lawmakers’ conduct. And she flagged the case as a sensitive matter that might
implicate politicians in the future.

In the summer of 2024, Kate Fifield, a prosecutor in the Justice Department’s
anti-corruption section, had been assigned to join the case. Fifield was
wrapping up [a high-profile prosecution](https://www.justice.gov/usao-
dc/pr/retired-us-navy-admiral-sentenced-six-years-bribery-scheme) of a retired
Navy admiral who traded a government contract for a future job. Turning her
attention to Kao, she and the FBI agents weighed their options. They
considered getting high-level approval to deploy undercover agents. Proving an
exchange of cash for favors often requires the kind of inconvertible evidence
that undercover recordings can provide.

But before the investigation took flight, the new Trump administration began
to demolish the Justice Department. The president’s handpicked leaders ordered
prosecutors to drop a corruption case against New York Mayor Eric Adams,
triggering [a wave of resignations](https://abcnews.com/Politics/new-yorks-
top-federal-prosecutor-steps-amid-tension/story?id=118796725) in the Public
Integrity Section where Fifield worked, and revoked the section’s authority to
bring new cases.

Then Trump’s FBI director, Kash Patel, began to purge the anti-corruption unit
in the Washington D.C., field office, where many agents had investigated
Trump.

Ball was fired in October 2025. Kevin Gounaud, another agent who had been
working with her on the investigation, was pushed out in early 2026. Through
their lawyer, the agents declined to comment.

The corruption investigation, just launched, suddenly went dark.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Pay-for-play-
Beatrice-Caciotti_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **The
FBI Anti-Corruption Squad Was Circling Susan Collins — Until Trump Got in the
Way** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/fbi-susan-collins-navatek-campaign-
donations-investigation)

The White House referred ProPublica’s questions to the FBI and DOJ.

The Department of Justice didn’t respond to detailed questions about the
investigation.

“Under President Trump, the Justice Department is rooting out the
weaponization, corruption, and institutional rot that ran rampant under Joe
Biden’s two-tiered system of justice,” DOJ spokesperson Audrey Cook said.

Kao’s claims are “half baked” and “misleading,” FBI spokesperson Ben
Williamson said. “Additionally, as we have said repeatedly, personnel are only
removed at this FBI if they have been found to have acted unethically,
undermined the mission, or engaged in weaponization of law enforcement.”

Meanwhile, Integer has rapidly expanded. Last year, it reported $81 million in
contracts and [announced](https://www.integer-tech.com/integer-technologies-
adds-63-million-in-annual-economic-impact-for-south-carolina/) that number
would climb to $375 million by 2030. The company inked partnership deals with
universities in New Hampshire, Louisiana and Mississippi. The University of
South Carolina called its partnership with the firm a “model for public-
private success.”  
  
The company continues to forge ties with powerful politicians. In late 2024,
